name: Vardan Mamikonian
otherNames: Vartan the Great, by a note in Victor Langlois's edition of Lazar of Pharp
knownFor: General of the Armenians who, after yielding in outward show at the Persian court, led the Armenian rising against the Persian king's religion and fell at Avarayr in 451, remembered by the Armenian church as a martyr.
dates: Fell at Avarayr in 451, by Elishe and Lazar of Pharp. Malachia Ormanian gives the day as 26 May; Charles Neumann's margin and a note in Lazar's French edition give 2 June. No source used here gives his birth
place: Armenia; the Persian court; Avarayr, on the plain of the Deghmut
role: General of the Armenians and lord of the Mamikonian house

traces: Elishe's History is the History of Vartan and of the battle of the Armenians, written, its dedication says, at the request of the priest David of the Mamikonian house.
Elishe and Lazar of Pharp count one thousand and thirty-six Armenians who fell with him.
remembered: Lazar of Pharp: God gave him "le titre de martyr, qui devait durer éternellement parmi toutes les nations".
Malachia Ormanian: the Armenian calendar commemorates the martyrs of Avarayr "on Shrove-Thursday", and lists "Vardan and his thousand and thirty-five companions" among the saints.

uncertain: His words, the refusal at court and the speech before Avarayr, come only as Elishe and Lazar of Pharp wrote them. Both write for the Armenian side and tell the fallen as martyrs.

The day of Avarayr is given two ways. Malachia Ormanian, a former Armenian patriarch of Constantinople writing in the twentieth century, gives 26 May 451. Charles Neumann's margin, and a note in the French edition of Lazar, give 2 June 451.

That he gave way at the Persian court in outward show, and why, is Lazar of Pharp's account, told at length. Elishe says that some of the princes, on a royal councillor's advice, sent word that they would conform.
That Sahak the Great was his grandfather and teacher rests on Lazar of Pharp, in a rough French scan, and on Charles Neumann's preface to Elishe.
